questions.q: Why does the low-and-slow exfiltration in this case study evade volume-based data-loss detection?
options: The transfers only happen outside business hours, when monitoring is disabled
The data is encrypted, which makes volume-based detection technically impossible
Each individual transfer is small enough to stay under any volume threshold, even though the cumulative pattern over time is abnormal
Volume-based detection was never configured on this network at all
questions.explain: Low-and-slow exfiltration is deliberately sized to stay under per-transfer thresholds, which is exactly why baseline/pattern detection is needed instead.

questions.q: What specifically does the NetFlow baseline deviation flag in this case, if not the size of any transfer?
options: A sudden drop in overall network bandwidth
A brand-new destination this host has never contacted before, reached on a suspiciously regular interval
The total number of employees using the network that day
The specific content of the files being transferred
questions.explain: The flow platform flags the pattern — a new host-destination pair with unusual regularity — not the volume of any single transfer.

questions.q: In the process tree WINWORD.EXE -> cmd.exe -> svch0st.exe, what is the actual giveaway that this is malicious?
options: The process name mimics svchost.exe but runs from a user-writable temp folder instead of System32
Word documents can never legitimately open a command shell under any circumstances
The process tree shows more than two levels of parent-child relationships
cmd.exe is inherently malicious software
questions.explain: Masquerading relies on a familiar-looking name; the real tell is the process running from a location the genuine system process never would.

questions.q: Why is a threat-intel-flagged destination IP described as "a lead, not proof" on its own?
options: Because threat intel only applies to email-based attacks, not network traffic
Because IP addresses can never be legitimately associated with malicious infrastructure
Because threat intelligence feeds are never accurate enough to use in a SOC
Because intel feed entries can be stale or imprecise, so a match alone doesn't confirm malicious activity without corroborating signals
questions.explain: A flagged IP raises suspicion but needs to be combined with other signals, like the flow deviation and EDR telemetry, to become actionable.

questions.q: What is the correct first containment action once all three signals confirm the exfiltration?
options: Isolate the host via EDR, cutting its network access without disturbing evidence running in memory
Immediately reimage the workstation from a clean backup
Delete the suspicious binary before any other analysis is done
Wait for the next scheduled vulnerability scan to confirm the finding
questions.explain: EDR-based isolation stops further data loss and lateral movement while preserving the running evidence needed for full analysis.
